en: Sūtra: Mahākāśyapa went to visit him and inquire after his illness. The commentary states: There are three parts to the concluding words;
here, they collectively present the exhaustion of the Way. Kāśyapa specializes in relieving the poor and suffering, yet he cannot bestow compassion equally;
he still maintains the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*), yet he cannot be without marks in every action. Because of this, he was put to the test; therefore, he did not respond.
Enduring.
Regarding the passage from "For what reason? up to "he went and wandered for alms," the commentary says:
In the second section below, the ultimate nature of reality is specifically revealed; first, there is the inquiry, followed by the revelation.
Within the revelation, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of one's own realization, and second, the citation of another's words.
This question and the account of his own experience concern this matter.

When he wandered through poor and humble alleys to beg in accordance with custom, it was because those in poverty do not cultivate themselves; thus they remain poor and may even fall further into destitution, so he exhorted them.
Since the wealthy are not like this, he did not beg from them.
The wealthy possess abundance in overflowing measure; when they give, it accords with their own disposition and is plentiful.
The poor lack all means; when they give, it is contrary to their inclinations and obtained only with difficulty.

Since the purpose of wealth is fundamentally to support oneself and benefit others, rather than seeking to increase one's own hoard, there is a specific reason for wandering through the alleys of the poor.
Because he went on his alms-round in successive order, it is called "cultivation.
The sutra says:
At that time, Vimalakīrti arrived and spoke these words.
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the words of others.
There are two parts:
First, the preliminary exposition of the principles; second, the formal presentation of the discourse.
This is the first section.
Scripture: "Only Mahākāśyapa... begging from the poor."
The commentary states:
First, the erroneous nature of the matter is restated; second, the correct principle is set forth; and finally, the conclusion offers an exhortation.
This is the first section of that text.
When begging from the poor, causing them to become wealthy and happy is *maitrī* (loving-kindness);
uprooting their poverty and suffering is *karuṇā* (compassion).
Since this only provides relief for the poor while excluding the noble, the powerful, and the wealthy, it is said that [this practice] is not universal.
Sūtra: When the Venerable Kāśyapa arrived, it was his turn to go on alms-round.
Commentary: The following sets forth the correct principle.
The text further consists of two parts:
first, the petitioner; second, the donor.
Within the section on the petitioner, the text further contains three parts:
First, the refutation of the six characteristics; second, the guarding of the six sense faculties; and third, the elucidation of realizing the principle and cultivating the cause.

Regarding the first, the refutation of the six characteristics: (1) refuting biased conduct; (2) setting forth the perception of food; (3) dispelling the appearance of villages; (4) destroying the appearance of city colors; (5) proceeding toward the state of the Buddha-family; and (6) refuting attachment to appearances.
This refutes partiality in practice.
One should beg only from the poor, so that the poor may become wealthy;
one should not beg from the wealthy, so that the wealthy may become poor.
Therefore, abiding in equanimity, one should practice alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*).
The old translation lacks six items and contains only four; it omits "entering towns and villages" and "approaching the households of Buddhas.
The sūtra states: "For the sake of non-eating, one should practice alms-gathering."
The commentary states:
This section eliminates the notion of food.
Kāśyapa perceived that there was still the appearance of food; since he sought to sustain his body solely for the purpose of relieving the poor, he proceeded next to beg for alms.
Now, one practices begging for alms based on three meanings; it is not merely for the sake of sustaining the body and so forth.
First, because even upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood and attaining *bodhi*, one still does not require food, one practices begging for alms to sustain the *dharmakāya*.
Second, in order to destroy the long-standing attachment to the food of birth and death, one should practice begging for alms to break through that cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "When eating morsel food, it should be regarded as like the flesh of one's own son in the wilderness," and so forth.
Third, he practices begging for alms in order to receive offerings from others, so that they may fulfill the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Among these three causes, the first is the cause for his own six perfections; the second is the severing of the bonds of birth and death; and the third is the fulfillment of the six perfections of others. It is for these three purposes that he practices begging for alms.

In the original text, the second [section] was intended to destroy the characteristic of composite phenomena (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*) in order to eliminate attachment to food, because food is a composite phenomenon consisting of the three sensory objects.
The third [section], concerning "not receiving," should have followed the passage on the characteristic of the empty village (*śūnyagrāma-lakṣaṇa*), yet it is now placed after that.
The sequence of the old sūtra differs from that of the new one; it lacks the third phrase found here.
Sūtra: "With the perception of an empty village, he enters various cities and towns.
Commentary: [As follows:]
Within this, there are two parts: first, the elimination of the perception of villages; second, the destruction of the perception of towns and cities.
When entering various villages and settlements, one should perceive them as empty villages and not see them as villages.
Because others see me contemplating the Triple Gem, they cease evil and apply themselves to good; there are ten benefits [to this], and thus I enter cities and towns.
I benefit these sentient beings, and not for any other reason.
Sūtra: One should form the thought of approaching the Buddha’s household and then accept that food.
Commentary: There are two [types of] intermediate existence (*antarābhava*):
First, the aspect of entering a Buddha-family; second, the aspect of destroying attachment.

Regarding "Buddha-family": when one enters the house of a donor within the Buddha-dharma realm, one should conceive of it as entering the home of True Reality—signless and unconditioned—and thus accept their food for the purpose of destroying attachment.
"To not receive" means to be without attachment.
Furthermore, the purity of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*) and the emptiness of the substance of the three factors is called "not receiving.
This is because both the subject that receives and the object received are termed "receiving."
Above, one breaks the six marks; below, one guards the six sense faculties. This point was already explained above regarding the errors in the old translations.
The Sūtra states: "What is seen reaches up to being realized through wisdom.
The commentary says:
The second passage below concerns the prevention and blocking of the six sense faculties.
This refers to the prevention of the five [physical] faculties.
Seeing forms as if one were blind, not perceiving beauty or ugliness, how could attachment or aversion arise?
Hearing sounds is like an echo; they are not real sounds, so who is there to praise or revile?
Smelling fragrances is like the wind; it contains no judgment of good or bad, so who can be increased or diminished by them? Who can be made more virtuous or more evil?
Regarding the flavors one consumes, one does not discriminate between their bitterness, sourness, sweetness, or pungency; who is there to be cherished?
Who is there to be rejected?
When experiencing various tactile objects, it is like a wise person realizing the truth: their characteristics cannot be described or discriminated—what is smooth? What is rough?
Therefore, one guards the five sense faculties so that they do not give rise to transgressions.
The Sūtra says: "One knows that all dharmas are like illusory appearances, up to [the realization that] there is no extinction.
The Commentary states:
This is the guarding of the faculty of mind.

When consciousness penetrates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one thereby realizes that suffering and pleasure are of a single flavor. One understands that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) have the characteristic of being like an illusion; they are not real, arising falsely through causes and conditions, lacking any inherent activity, and not produced from themselves.
There is no intrinsic nature and no activity by another; it does not arise from another and possesses no other-nature; it does not arise from both together and possesses no nature of self or other.
Although these three do not exist, they possess functional efficacy through the conditions of their activity, for such conditions can be apprehended.

For this reason, it is said that there is no truly burning cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), nor is there a quiescent nirvāṇa; both are of a single flavor and are thus equally identical. Why, then, should the consciousness engage in various conceptual discriminations?
The ancient sutra states: "Fundamentally, it has never been ignited; originally, there is no birth-and-death.
Now, there is neither extinction nor nirvana. The meaning and intent are identical [to the present teaching].
Sūtra: When the Venerable Kāśyapa arrived, he was able to obtain food.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the third section, which clarifies the cultivation of the causes for realizing the principle.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of equality; second, the conclusion regarding what may be eaten.
This is the initial passage.
The first and second [sections] each have two parts:
first, equality in principle; second, equality in practice.

As for the eight wrongs, these are the wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong effort, which are produced by non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings.

The eight liberations are those arising from the noble ones of the Buddha-dharma: first, possessing form, one perceives forms; second, being internally without form, one perceives external forms; third, personally realizing the pure liberation; fourth, the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the liberation of cessation.
These eight liberations have already been explained as before.

Regarding "not abandoning the eight," one may give rise to them by conforming to the ways of non-Buddhists for the purpose of subduing them; thus, one enters the eight liberations which correctly accord with the true path.

Furthermore, when false and correct principles are equal, one enters the true equality of the dharma-nature by means of the equality of all phenomena with the false; this equality of dharma-nature is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
The above points are all meanings that accord with reason.
The principle of emptiness states:
because the objective realm is fundamentally empty, the forms perceived are like those seen by the blind;
because dependent origination is not substantially existent, it is like an illusory appearance.

All phenomena are non-dual; both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal, and the false and the correct are no different. Therefore, by means of the equality of the false, one can enter the equality of the correct.
All these are ultimate truths, for all are signless and their nature is emptiness.
The preceding section clarifies that the principles of the heterodox and the orthodox are equal; the following section clarifies that the matters of making offerings are equal.

By offering a single morsel of food to the Buddhas and the worthy sages of the ten directions, one cultivates the causal practice of equanimity; though this act is small, the fruit obtained is boundless.
Sūtra: "One who eats in this manner may then eat. Commentary:
This concludes the section on what may be eaten.
Not abiding in defilement or purity, not abiding in concentration or distraction, and not abiding in rising or sinking is called the "non-abiding path.
That which has obstructions is called "defiled," while that which is untainted is called "free from defilement."
Because the untainted (anāsrava) is already perfected, it is not characterized by defilement;
because the tainted (sāsrava) manifests, it is not devoid of defilement.
The old translation "affliction" (kleśa) is incorrect.
Engaging in altruistic deeds externally does not mean one has entered meditative concentration;
maintaining a mind that is never distracted does not mean one has emerged from meditative concentration.
With great wisdom fully perfected, having already attained nirvana, one does not abide in the cycle of birth and death.
Because Great Compassion is already fulfilled and he constantly brings benefit and happiness to others, he does not abide in nirvana.
Only when one attains this non-abiding may one eat;
this is the meaning that accords with reason.
The principle of emptiness states:
because within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there are no characteristics that can be characterized, it is not possessed of defilement;
yet, because it does not abandon the worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in its work of benefiting sentient beings, it is not devoid of defilement.
"Even to the point of not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, yet abiding in this ultimate truth while not abandoning conventional truth—only then may you eat.
Sūtra: "All those who give to the Venerable One... up to those who do not incline toward the state of a śrāvaka."
The commentary states: Regarding "the superior presentation of the petitioner" and "the superior presentation of giving":

not being attached to the self-substance, not being attached to the karmic retribution, and not being attached to the repayment of kindness is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Therefore, there is no attainment of the small fruits of humans, devas, or the two vehicles, nor the great fruits of Bodhisattvas or Tathāgatas in future lives.
Not giving rise to wrong views that slander cause and effect, nor practicing faithless giving, is called "absence of diminution.
Not giving rise to false attachments to a self or phenomena is called "absence of augmentation."
Regarding the "path to Buddhahood": because Nirvana and True Suchness (tathatā) are empty of three things, when one practices giving, one proceeds toward this path to Buddhahood.
The True Suchness of Great Parinirvāṇa and the Buddha-nature do not lead to the stage of a Śrāvaka.
Sūtra: When the Venerable Kāśyapa arrived at the place where food was being offered, he praised it, saying:
"This concludes the third section, which summarizes and exhorts."

Based on what has been explained above, by shattering the six marks and guarding the six sense faculties, one enters the cause of equality; because of this solemn exposition of the Great [Vehicle], one does not eat in vain, becomes a field of merit, and brings benefit to both self and others.

If one possesses these six characteristics, fails to guard the six sense faculties, and does not enter into equanimity, then because their practice is so limited, they merely consume food in vain; they are not a true field of merit, and both themselves and others are harmed.
At that time, our World-Honored One, having aroused a heart of profound reverence, praised him, saying:
"This is the third greatness. This concludes the response, as he requested to withdraw with humble body.
There are five parts:

first, clarifying that by hearing the supreme Dharma one attains what was never before attained; second, manifesting the profound arising of a reverential mind toward the Bodhisattva; third, praising his wisdom and eloquence; fourth, manifesting one's own progress and benefit; and fifth, providing a concluding summary in response.
Regarding these first two passages of the Sūtra,
from "How marvelous, World-Honored One" up to "the mind of perfect enlightenment," the commentary says:
This praises his wisdom and eloquence.
It is a cause for wonder that even a layperson engaged in the affairs of a household can attain such a state;
were it a monastic, it would not be a matter for marvel, as such progress is already within their own sphere of practice.
"What wise person, upon hearing this sublime Dharma, would not resolve their mind toward Great Awakening?
[The Sūtra says: "From that time forth, I have come to visit him to inquire after his illness.
[The Commentary] states:
This reveals the benefits already attained and serves as a concluding summary of the answer.
The Sūtra says: At that time, the World-Honored One went to inquire after his illness.
The Commentary states:
The fourth section below begins with the command to question.
In Sanskrit he is called Mahāsudatta, which here means "Great Sudatta," as he was well able to manifest his birth during the time of the Buddha.
Some had previously made great vows and were now able to manifest them before their eyes, thoroughly comprehending the meaning of emptiness.
Or there was a great elder in the city of Śrāvastī named Kula, who obtained [the child] through prayers to the heavens.
At the time of his birth, the chamber was empty and tranquil.
An interpreter of signs divined it and named him Sudarśana;
"Darśana" means "birth."

At the time of his birth, the room was entirely empty and still, signifying that as he grew up, he would skillfully understand the meaning of emptiness; therefore, he was named Subhūti (Excellent Manifestation).
At that time, the Great Subhūti went to him to inquire about his illness.
The commentary states:
This is a general presentation of the exhaustion of the path.
Although Subhūti practices alms-gathering with equanimity, he has not yet realized the Dharma of emptiness; thus, his principle remains unequal.

Although he was without dispute in his conduct while entering villages to beg for food, his realization of the principle of non-dispute was not yet perfected; therefore, he was rebuked and replied that he was incapable. Thus it is said in the Sūtra.
Why is this so? It leads up to his subsequent entry into the house.
The commentary states:
"Below, the principle is specifically revealed through its ultimate exhaustion; first there is the inquiry, followed by the revelation."
The clarification has two parts:
first, the presentation of one's own position; second, the presentation of another's words.
This [section] constitutes the inquiry and the presentation of one's own position.
[Sūtra] After some time, Vimalakīrti arrived and said to me:
[Commentary] The following section reveals the words of another.
There are two parts:
first, clarifying the arrival at the refutation; second, the actual presentation of the argument.
This is the initial passage.
Sūtra: Only when the Venerable Subhūti has arrived may you take the food.
Commentary:
Below, the formal address is set forth.
Within this, there are six parts: first, stating the principle;
second, revealing one's own delusion; third, clarifying another's consolation; fourth, manifesting one's own response; fifth, recounting another's instruction; and sixth, accomplishing benefit.
The initial section further consists of four parts:

first, manifesting the equality of the Dharma-Buddha; second, manifesting the equality of bondage and liberation; third, manifesting the equality of the heterodox and the orthodox; and fourth, manifesting the equality of good and evil.
This is the initial passage.
There are four kinds of nutriment, as previously explained.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness, it says:
This equality is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Since food is the root of causes and conditions, one uses food as a point of reference; through the principle of the emptiness of food, one enters into the emptiness of all phenomena.
Food is a particular phenomenon, while the rest are general phenomena; both are empty.
Through the principle of the emptiness of all phenomena, one enters the principle of the Buddha’s emptiness; apart from this emptiness, there is no separate emptiness of the Buddha.
One who thoroughly understands this emptiness, whose mind is free from attachment, whose actions are impartial and equal, and who possesses purity, may then accept food.
Subhūti has not yet realized this emptiness; his mind still harbors attachments, and he lacks impartiality and purity. How, then, could he accept food?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"This equality is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). To understand food as suchness is to understand the suchness of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
To understand the suchness of all phenomena is to understand the suchness of the Buddha."
From the subtle to the manifest, one attains the understanding of the nature of equality; when the wisdom of realization arises, the mind is free from attachment.
For the sake of benefiting others, one may partake of food only after practicing external equanimity and purity.
This is not so; how else could one be said to consume food in vain?

The older translation equates the two—the equality of food and the equality of the Dharma—such that they are mutually identical, yet it lacks the equality of the Buddha; thus, it omits the principle and contradicts the text.
Sūtra: From the Venerable Subhūti’s arrival at entering the path of a single destination, the commentary states:
Below this is the second [section], the equality of bondage and liberation.
There are nine pairs in total; among these, there are two:
first, the pair of the wholesome and the unwholesome; second, the pair of the view of self and the view of non-self.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness, it is said:
When the mind engages in conceptual differentiation, bondage and liberation are treated as two.
Because one realizes ultimate truth, the conceptual differentiations of the mind regarding bondage and liberation are non-dual, for both are empty in principle.
This is the meaning that accords with reason:

Because there is great benefit in manifesting the practice of unwholesome roots without severing them—just as King Tuṣita manifested the teaching and so forth—he does not actually cause others to hold the *kuśāstra* (heretical) views; this is termed the "false view of a self-body" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) or the "view of a self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Those who do not destroy the view of self manifest its arising;
for they seek great enlightenment and deliver sentient beings all for the sake of the "self," yet they enter the path of the single destination of non-self.
The principle of non-self is called "the single destination" (*ekāyana*), for it is that to which practitioners of all three vehicles collectively return.
The "path" is the cognitive faculty; it is the vision of non-self, through which one abandons the vision of self and realizes the vision of non-self.
"Entering" means awakening to the meaning.
What was formerly called "not destroying the body" refers to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
"Following a single characteristic" refers to the view of non-self (anātman-dṛṣṭi).
Within the view of non-self, there is nothing further, as there are no two [distinct entities].
The Sūtra says: "From the non-extinction of ignorance up to liberation.
The commentary states:
Among these, one pair—defilement attaining purity—is opposed to ignorance as the cause for initiating karma.

"Existence" refers to the three realms of existence (*bhava*), while "craving" refers to craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*). Existence and craving are precisely the conditions that moisten rebirth; this is because they constitute the root of the bondage of birth and death.
Accommodating all sentient beings and not abandoning birth and death, it is therefore said that [ignorance] is not extinguished.
Although ignorance is not extinguished, the light of untainted wisdom arises;
although craving for existence is not extinguished, liberation arises.
Although liberation (vimukti) serves as the condition for moistening rebirth, it is a category of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) because it realizes the unconditioned principle (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Since the realized true reality is called liberation, it is none other than nirvāṇa.
Sūtra: "One is able to reach the equality of the dharma-nature through the absence of interval. Commentary:
Herein, there is one pair, namely, the pair of suffering and pleasure.
"Avīci" refers to the Avīci Hell, cited here as a place of ultimate suffering.
"Liberation" refers to Nirvana, a place of ultimate bliss.
This is because one enters the *tathatā* (suchness) of ultimate bliss by means of the *tathatā* of ultimate suffering, for their essence is of a single flavor.

The old translation states, "One attains liberation through the characteristics of the five heinous crimes. It should rather be said that the characteristics of the fruit of the five heinous crimes enter into the characteristics of liberation, because these are none other than True Suchness (Tathatā).
Sūtra: "Neither liberated nor bound, up to being free from the dharmas of ordinary beings.
Commentary:
This consists of three pairs.
First, regarding the opposition between liberation and bondage: that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called liberation, while that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) is called bondage.
To realize *nirvāṇa* is called being without bondage; not abandoning *saṃsāra* is called being without liberation.

Second, the distinction between realization and non-realization: truly seeing the truths is called "realization"; therefore, it is said that one does not fail to see. Not seeing is called "non-realization," because at the time of realizing the principle, there is no characteristic of [subjective] vision.
The three fruits are not opposed to being fruits.

Those called "noble" (ārya) have attained the fruits; yet because they remain in accordance with the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and do not abide exclusively in the fruits, they are said not to have attained the fruits [in that specific sense].
Those who are not noble are called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); since they have already realized the true path, they are no longer ordinary beings.

He constantly teaches and transforms those who delight in giving rise to afflictions; therefore, it is said that one does not attain the fruit by being separated from the dharmas of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Although this forms a pair [with the preceding statement], it reveals that the one of great compassion accords with *saṃsāra*; since *saṃsāra* exists within the state of an ordinary person, the term "not separated" is repeated for emphasis.
Sūtra: One may take food only after [the recipient] has reached the state of being non-saintly (*asaṃskṛta*). Commentary:
Within this, there are two pairs.
First, the contrast between the ordinary and the holy:
Great Compassion accords with the ordinary, and is thus called "not holy";
yet, having already realized the supramundane, it is called "not unholy."
Second is the realization of detachment from oppositions.
Because one realizes all dharmas, it is called "accomplishment";
because one severs the conceptualization and clinging to the notion of those dharmas, it is called "detachment."
The preceding discussion was based on the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), hence this interpretation was formulated.

Alternatively, these [passages] may all be explaining that the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is empty, impermanent, and so forth; or they may simply be explaining that the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is the equality of ultimate truth. In either case, there is no contradiction in principle.
Sūtra: "Venerable Subhūti, you may take food only when [the conditions] have been met.
Commentary: From here below is the third section, on the equality of the heterodox and the orthodox.
The *Kongliyi* states:
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is a duality of the false and the true, wherein one abandons the false to return to the true.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no duality between the false and the true; what, then, is there to abandon and what is there to return to?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "Those who see me by means of form, or seek me by means of sound, follow a deviant path and do not see the Tathāgata."
The Three Jewels of the same essence (sahaja-triratna) cannot be seen or heard, nor can they be served or worshipped.
In the older translations, there is no mention of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the six heretical teachers, they were the superior conditions for skillful means by which the Buddha attained Bodhi; if you, like the Buddha, take them as your teachers, then because they have actually fallen into the evil realms due to their false views, you—out of compassion for them—must likewise fall into the evil realms to provide salvation.
Only one who is identical to the Tathāgata may take this food.
Subhūti the Great has abandoned those six teachers; he cannot follow their teachings, nor does he neglect sentient beings by following them into the evil realms.
Seeing that there are the Three Jewels, yet failing to realize their identity as one essence, he now departs for whom?
As for the six teachers: the first is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.

*Kāśyapa* is his nature and *Pūraṇa* is his name; the ancients called him Pūranakāśyapa. He is a non-Buddhist of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), also known as a proponent of the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*).
The second is Makkhali Gosāla.

"Makkhali" is his own name, while "Gosāla" is the name of his mother; as he was the son of Gosālā, he is distinguished by her name. What was formerly called Māgandiya Kūṭadanta is actually the eternalist (sassatavādin) non-Buddhist.
Third is Vatsīputra.

"Vatsī" is his own name, while "Putra" is the name of his mother; he is called the son of that woman, just as Śāriputra [is called the son of Śārī]. He is also known as Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, which was translated in ancient times as "the son of Sañjaya Vairāṭī," namely the non-Buddhist ascetic who practiced austerities.
He taught that the birth and death loved by sentient beings are all caused by attachment to pleasure, and that through the diligent practice of asceticism one attains liberation.
He was called Ajita Keśakambala;

"Ajita" is his name, and because he wore long hair and a coarse woolen garment (*kambala*), he was termed "Keśakambala. The ancients called him Ajita Keśakambala; he was a naturalist heretic who taught that all phenomena arise spontaneously.
Pañcaśikha. "Gāyana" is a clan name, while "Śikha" refers to a physical form;
because there is a protuberance on the crown of his head like that of an ox's head, he was named accordingly.
An ancient tradition states: "Kātyāyana Kālāmas was one who followed Mahādeva; he taught that Mahādeva is able to give rise to all phenomena."
"The Great Nirgrantha-putra" refers to this Nirgrantha.
Because he adheres to the ascetic practices of his original teacher, he is called a "Nirgrantha" (Fetterless One).
Since he was born from him, he is called a "son" (putra). Thus, he is known as the "Great Nirgrantha-putra."

This refers to the heretics who advocate the doctrine of past actions as the cause; they claim that all phenomena have their causes already established in previous lives, and that by no longer creating new causes and exhausting old karma, one immediately attains liberation.
The ancients said: "Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

This is the summons.
In Sanskrit he is called Upāli, which here means "Near-Attendant" (Jin-zhi).
When the Buddha was a crown prince, he served as his close minister, managing affairs of state; thus he is called "Near-Attendant," which refers to the official in charge of the treasury.
The Śākyas who had renounced the world left behind their garments, jeweled crowns, and elephants, bestowing them all upon him.
Later, he reflected:
"Even the sons of the Śākyas, though of noble and wealthy status, have abandoned their homes to go forth."
"What kind of person am I that I still remain at ease?
He hung his crown upon a tree and tied his elephant between the branches, making this vow:
"Whoever takes these, I shall offer them as a gift."
He went to where the sons of the Śākyas were and recounted his intentions in full.
The sons of the Śākyas were all delighted and came to inform the Buddha:
"Please allow him to be ordained first so that he may be our senior; once he has abandoned his pride, we shall serve him with respect."
The Buddha granted his permission; the Śākya son paid his respects and prostrated before Upāli, whereupon the great earth shook.
A voice from the sky praised him from afar:
"The mountain of pride of these princes has collapsed."
"By humbling oneself, one honors others first; now, let this humble form suffice as a greeting.
Because he was the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya, he was now summoned.
At that time, Upāli arrived at his dwelling to inquire after his illness.
The commentary states:
There are three parts to the following passage. First, it generally describes the failure of the Way.
I act in accordance with the Vinaya to instruct him to cease his transgressions; he speaks of realizing the Truth, and only then will the seeds of his offenses be extinguished.
I maintain that one eliminates transgressions through body and speech, whereas he claims that defilements are exhausted only by realizing the source of the mind.
Since his reasoning has fallen, his argument is also defeated; thus, this concludes the discussion.
Sūtra: "Why is this so? up to "...dare not [speak of] the Buddhas.
Commentary: The following clarifies that the principle has reached its ultimate limit.
There are two parts:
first, the presentation of one's own account; second, the citation of another's words.
Within the presentation of one's own account, there are two further sections:
First, the two individuals come to request the removal of their offenses; subsequently, it is explained that they have properly extinguished them according to the Dharma.
Within the section where the two individuals first come to request the removal of their offenses, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the reason for their arrival; second, clarifying the ritual procedure for their arrival; and third, the actual request for the removal of the offense.
This is the initial passage.

The Buddha is the Lord of the Dharma, his majestic virtue being uniquely supreme; thus, even a minor matter or a slight offense would truly be unacceptable, and so [the disciple], harboring shame and embarrassment, did not dare to approach the Buddha.
The Sūtra says: "He came to where I was and spoke to me.
The Commentary states:
This clarifies the proper manner of arrival.
Sūtra: Only Upāli was able to escape this fault. Commentary:
This is a request for absolution from transgression.
I feel great fear regarding even minor transgressions.
Having violated the rules of conduct, I am truly ashamed.
I pray that you will dispel the anxiety in my heart and the remorse in my mind, so that I may be freed from these faults.
Since the offense was pardonable, it was clear that it did not constitute a primary transgression.
I then acted as his advocate to request the opportunity for him to be transformed.
The eulogy says:
The following explains how to pacify [an offense] in accordance with the Dharma.
"In accordance with the Dharma" means according to the Vinaya rules.
The Blessed One has established light regulations for serious matters, or established serious regulations for light matters.

However, at the time of emerging from an offense, it is merely a formal ritual; this is how it ought to be according to principle. It is not a method for extinguishing the offense through the path of karma (*karmapatha*). Rather, as explained according to the principles of the Vinaya, it serves to eliminate remorse and purify the transgression committed.
Sūtra: Manifestation, Exhortation, Encouragement, and Consolation. Commentary:

These reveal the characteristics of reality as they are: first, manifestation; second, exhortation; third, encouragement; and fourth, consolation. Other sūtras also add "causing one to become free from desire."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states: "To cause those who seek freedom from desire to do so, one censures the six types of unwholesome (*kṛṣṇa*) practices, demonstrating their faults and disadvantages in order to bring about detachment from craving and defilement."
This is what was taught:
to eliminate grief and regret.
As for "demonstrating," it means showing the four kinds of true principles in order to cause others to undertake and train in the conduct of purity.

"Exhortation" refers to having already manifested the attainment of faith and understanding, establishing [the practitioner] in the precepts, and causing them to correctly undertake and practice them, because one has attained mastery over that [attainment].
He then requested, saying:
"What should I do now? I only pray that you will instruct me on how to repent."
Thereupon, he addressed them, saying:
"Regarding such matters as these, you should act and train yourselves accordingly.

As for "encouragement," it means that if they should give rise to despondency in their minds regarding what is to be known, what is to be practiced, or what is to be attained, one then praises and exhorts their minds at that time, enabling them to possess the power and capacity for those tasks.

"Consolation" means that if one practices with courageous and correct application toward the Dharma and that which accords with the Dharma, one should accordingly praise and express joy as it truly is, causing them to rejoice.
There is another interpretation, which is consistent with that treatise: herein, it means causing one to be free from the defilement of transgressions.

It indicates the category of purity (*śukla-pakṣa*), exhorts toward right practice, praises [the practitioner] so they do not regress, and celebrates their deeds to inspire joy; this is called "speaking in accordance with the Dharma."
This was omitted from the old translation of the sutra. When Vimalakīrti arrived, he spoke these words.
[The] Commentary says:
The following clarifies the words of others.
This section has two parts:
first, explaining the approach to the ritual; second, formally presenting the words.
This is the opening passage of the sutra:
"Only Upāli... do not disturb his mind.
The commentary says:

There are five parts to the formal petition: first, the removal of opposing arguments; second, the manifestation of praise; third, the clarification that the announcement has been made; fourth, the demonstration that the transgression has been extinguished; and fifth, the recitation of the aspiration.
Chen Li’s response is threefold:
first, a general refutation; second, the manifestation of the correct view; and third, the conclusion of the correct view.
This is the opening passage.
The *Kongliyi* (Meaning of the Principle of Emptiness) states:

When two people commit an offense, it arises from harboring the notion of existence (*saṃjñā*). Now, having requested repentance and removal, they are instead taught to give rise to existence once more; because there is an addition to what already exists, it is called "increasing the offense."

When you directly eliminate that mental remorse, you should explain for them that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty and signless (*animitta*) to dispel it; do not allow the notion of "having committed an offense" to disturb their minds.
"Disturbance" means chaos.
According to the meaning of the principle:

when two people commit an offense, the offense constitutes a karmic path (*karmapatha*); one must realize the essence of reality and penetrate its illusory nature in order to uproot the source of the offense.

If one merely relies on ritual procedures to perform the rite of extinction, speaking with the mouth while the heart remains contrary, then though extinguished it is not truly extinguished; karmic offenses are reborn, which is called "heavy increase.
One should instead preach the ultimate truth to enable them to realize it, and preach the conventional illusion to enable them to fully comprehend it; this is called "direct eradication."
Uproot the seeds of transgression; do not allow the mind to be disturbed by phenomenal signs (*nimitta*), thereby manifesting the extinction of offenses.
Why is this? [As stated in the Sūtra] up to: "It does not abide in either of the two."
The commentary states:
The following section on "Manifesting the Correct" has two parts. First, it clarifies ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to cause one to realize the root of transgression;

second, it clarifies conventional matters (*saṃvṛti*) to cause one to know the falsity of transgression. The passage beginning with "Only, Upāli, the nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-lakṣaṇa*) arises and ceases without abiding" constitutes the latter.
The characteristics of offenses have no reality and can easily be extinguished.
The root-seeds of offenses are fundamentally true; by realizing this, offenses are extinguished.
To extinguish offenses means to uproot the seeds of afflictions, evil karma, and the fruits of suffering.
Because the seeds are severed, one [type of] extinction occurs such that [the defilement] does not arise again;

this is called the confession of body and speech. However, it is merely termed "subjugation," which increases power and diminishes capacity, rather than being the true extinction of sin, for [the defilement] arises again later.
The beginning and middle [of this section] further consist of three parts:
first, the presentation of correct reasoning; second, the questioning that leads to understanding; and third, the clarification of the characteristics of defilement and purity.
There are three aspects to the presentation of reasoning:
First, the nature of sin is clarified; next, the basis of sin is clarified; finally, the substance of sin is clarified.
This is the initial passage.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
The nature of sin is the principle of true emptiness.
If the nature of sin were to exist, it could abide within the internal faculties, or arise from the external six objects, or be established in the interval between the two.
Since the nature of sin is fundamentally empty, where could it possibly abide?
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), offenses reside in the six sense faculties; because offenses arise with the six sense objects as conditions, they are also said to be "external.
As for internal causes and external conditions, they may reside within the six consciousnesses and so forth, which lie between the two.
Since the nature of sin is empty, it has no abode whatsoever.
When one realizes that the nature of sin is empty, what sin could there be?
The meaning according to principle is as follows:
The nature of sin is the principle of *tathatā* (suchness); this principle does not depend on internal faculties, external objects, or that which dwells between the two.
By contravening this principle, sins arise in succession.
Having realized this principle, one's offenses shall be eternally exhausted.
As stated in the Sūtra, from "As the Buddha has taught" up to "sentient beings are pure.
The commentary says:
This clarifies the basis of transgression.
There are two parts:

first, it clarifies that the person who commits the transgression is established in dependence upon the mind; second, it clarifies that the substance of the transgression arises only in dependence upon the mind, for a transgression must necessarily arise in dependence upon the mind.
This is the first passage.
"Offense" refers to unwholesome bodily karma that has been performed; its essence is the manifest and the seeds of unwholesome volition (*cetanā*).
The mind serves as its basis, because volition is that which depends [upon it].
Because it is subject to censure and loathing, it is called "sin.
Therefore, the text first clarifies the basis of sin so that one may thoroughly understand it, and only afterwards clarifies the essence of sin.
Before explaining the basis of sin, it first cites the Buddha’s words.
The Master Kongliyi says:
This citation refers to the teaching of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); "mind" here refers to the six consciousnesses, and it does not speak of eight.
If the mind were substantially existent and there were substantially existent transgressions, that would constitute the defilement of sentient beings.
The nature of the mind is fundamentally empty; since the sinner does not exist, sentient beings are pure.
The meaning according to reason is as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"Mind" refers to the eighth consciousness, and "sentient beings" refers to the provisional entity of the five aggregates, which is provisionally established based upon that mind.
If the eighth consciousness is contaminated and comprised of defilements, the provisional person who depends upon it is likewise defiled.
If the eighth consciousness, which serves as the basis, is uncontaminated and comprised of purity, the provisional person who depends upon it is likewise pure.
Now, this designation of a "sentient being" as a conceptual construct is based upon the eight consciousnesses, for the mind is the fundamental basis.
Therefore, both the offense and the offender do not exist apart from the mind.
Sūtra: "One whose mind is thus does not abide in the interval between [the two].
Commentary:
The following clarifies that the substance of transgression arises only by depending upon the mind.
The *Kongliyi* states:
"Such a mind, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), does not abide internally or externally, nor does it exist in between the two, because its nature is fundamentally empty."
It can give rise to the substance of transgression;
therefore, it is not real.
The meaning that accords with reason is as follows:

These eight consciousnesses are not the same as the six consciousnesses taught by the followers of the Two Vehicles. The six consciousnesses do not truly abide within the six sense organs, nor do they truly exist outside them or in between; they abide solely within the pure *dharmadhātu* of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and for this reason, even these defilements have no place of abiding.
Sūtra: "Just as their minds are thus, so too they do not transcend suchness.
Commentary:
This clarifies the essence of transgression.
The principle of emptiness states:
Just as its basis— the mind— is fundamentally empty and quiescent, with nothing at all upon which it dwells,
so too the defilements that depend upon it lack intrinsic nature within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) and have no locus of support.
Just as it is with the stains of transgression, so it is with all phenomena: who creates the conditions for transgression?
Who is the one who emerges from them?
Because the mind, transgression, and phenomena—these three—do not emerge from suchness, for suchness is like space and is non-existent.
The *Yinliyi* (Treatise on the Meaning of Rationality) states:
"Just as the fundamental mind does not abide in either the internal or external, but relies solely upon True Suchness (*tathatā*),
so too do the defilements that depend upon it rely upon Suchness, rather than abiding in the internal or external."

Just as with the stains of transgression, the conditions for committing an offense and the one who emerges from the offense—all phenomena likewise do not transcend suchness (*tathatā*). They do not depend on the internal or external; there is no real offense whatsoever, for everything is the principle of true suchness (*bhūtatathatā*).
Due to the delusion of the mind, various faults arise which are censurable and blameworthy; these are termed "sin.
Due to the awakening of the mind, sin is extinguished and goodness is produced; these are praiseworthy and joyful, and are termed "merit."
Therefore it is said: "Offenses arise from the mind and are extinguished by the mind.
Sūtra: "Only you, Upāli, have you ever been subject to defilement? Commentary:
[The Buddha] asked this.
The inquiry that brings about understanding has three parts: first, the question;
second, the answer; and third, the manifestation that brings about understanding.
This is the question.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
your mind is fundamentally pure because its nature is fundamentally empty; it is pure because it is free from defilement.
"When you attained the liberation of Arhat-nirvāṇa, was this mind of emptiness ever defiled?
Although there is a distinction between ordinary beings and sages, the mind itself is truly without difference; therefore, I ask this question."
The *Yili* (Principles of Correct Reasoning) states:
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the explanation of the purity of the nature of mind (*cittaprakṛti-viśuddhi*) briefly comprises two senses:
the first is the mind as suchness (*tathatā*) and dharmatā.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) yet being defiled is difficult to comprehend.

Regarding the mind of the two causes and conditions, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 54, explains that the mind of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not by nature affliction; it is termed "naturally pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*).
Now, because that mind is not itself an affliction, it is said to be pure by nature;
when it is associated with defilement, it is called a "defiled mind," but it is not the case that the essence of the mind is defiled and thus called a "defiled mind."
This mind is not only intrinsically pure by nature even before liberation is attained; it has likewise never been defiled at the time when liberation is attained.

Now, I ask only this: was that intrinsically pure mind ever defiled at the time it attained liberation? This is intended to demonstrate that, by analogy with the state of liberation, the mind’s nature is fundamentally pure even prior to liberation.
[Sutra]: "I said, 'No. [Commentary]:
This is the response.
At the time of attaining liberation, the mind has never been defiled.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*: "It is also like this.
Commentary:
This clarifies the principle for understanding emptiness:
having attained the realization of the noble ones and realized that the mind is fundamentally empty, one is therefore undefiled.
Therefore, one should know that the nature of the minds of sentient beings is fundamentally pure and has never been defiled; this is likewise because the mind is identical to emptiness.
The meaning according to principle is as follows:
by taking the causal-mind of ordinary beings as an analogy for the causal-mind of the sages, it is likewise fundamentally undefiled, because both share the same nature of mind.
From this it is known that evil thoughts are sins, like guests who arrive for a time and defile the mind;
once the wisdom of realization arises, these adventitious sins are extinguished.
Therefore, when the mind has severed the afflictions, it is called "freed from the bondage of association.
When it no longer takes objects as its cognitive support, it is called "freed from the bondage of the object.
Due to being freed from these two bondages, it is called "liberation of the mind."
Because one realizes and penetrates the principle, one penetrates the nature of the mind; this is called the extinction of offenses.
The Sūtra says: “Only Upāli... [until] its nature is intrinsically pure.
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the characteristics of defilement and purity.
Briefly, there are three sections; this is the first.
When the mind possesses general conceptualization and specific conceptualization, afflictions arise.
Because afflictions arise, sinful karma is consequently produced, which then brings about birth and death.

If there were neither general conceptualization nor specific conceptualization, there would be no afflictions; because afflictions would be absent, sinful karma would not arise, and one would thus attain purity and enter nirvana.
"Discrimination" refers to general discrimination;
"discrimination of difference" refers to various conceptual attachments.
Since you give rise to afflictions through these two, you should be free from discrimination in order to attain purity.
Sūtra: "If there is perversion... up to: its nature is intrinsically pure.
Commentary: This is the second turn [of the teaching].
Regarding "perversion" (*viparyāsa*): it refers to the grasping at true existence, permanence, bliss, self, and purity; because this turns one away from ultimate truth, it is called perversion.
Alternatively, there are seven perversions, which consist of these four plus three more: [perversion] of perception, mind, and view.
To give rise to conceptual construction and discrimination regarding those four is called the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
To find acceptance and pleasure in these four, and to establish and adhere to them, is called the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Regarding "perversion of mind," this refers to the afflictions such as craving that arise within those very objects of attachment; these are briefly categorized into three types:

first, those rooted in delusion; second, those whose intrinsic nature consists of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), a portion of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and craving (*rāga*); and third, those which are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of other afflictions.
As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, where these various inversions exist, there are afflictions; where these inversions are absent, one achieves purity.
Since you possess afflictions, it is evident that you have inversions.
Sūtra: "If there is grasping, it reaches the very nature of purity.
Commentary:
This is the third turn.
"Grasping" refers to the act of clinging; with the grasping at a self as its basis, defilement arises.
If one does not grasp at a self and realizes the non-existence of self, then one's nature is pure.
Since you are thus defiled, it is evident that there is grasping at a self;
this reveals the reason why those two types of people possess afflictions.
By causing one to realize the Truth above, the stains of sin will naturally perish.
The following section clarifies that worldly offenses are easy to extinguish, just as one knows that the conditions for a thief can easily be eliminated and destroyed.
Sūtra: "Only Upāli... like lightning, like clouds."
The commentary states:
The following clarifies mundane matters so that one may recognize sin and falsehood.
Briefly, there are four categories; this is the first.

Regarding the conventional arising and ceasing, there are briefly four similes: like illusions, transformations, lightning, and clouds; none of these are substantially existent, none abide, and their nature is inherently false.
Sūtra: "The nature of all phenomena reaches its end and does not abide even for a moment.
Commentary: This second section explains that conventional phenomena are swift; they have no expectation or waiting, do not endure through a single thought-moment, and perish immediately.
Sūtra: All dharmas are like a city of *gandharvas*. Commentary:
This third section explains that the substance of the conventional arises from false perception.
There are three similes for this:
it is like what is seen in a dream, because it arises from mental construction;
it is like a mirage, because craving arises and one grasps it as real water.

Regarding the "city of the gandharvas," this is translated as the "City of Fragrance-Seekers" (gandharvanagara). In the West, itinerant musicians are called "fragrance-seekers" (gandharva); they do not engage in productive labor but merely seek out the fragrance of food, performing music while waiting for alms from others.
This illusory city of transformation has lovely watchtowers and battlements, and is named Gandhavatī.
When the vapors from the ocean are struck by the rays of the sun, the distant sight of its crenellated walls also resembles an illusory city.
Water stirred up produces sound; when subtle, it is like music. Because it resembles that city of Gandharvas, it is also called the City of Gandharvas.
Since it arises through deception and delusion, it is used here as a metaphor.
Sūtra: "The nature of all dharmas reaches as far as an image in a mirror.
Commentary:
This fourth section explains that conventional mind acts like the moon reflected in water.
In reality, there is no moon in the water; it is the mind that delusively perceives one as being there. Failing to realize that the water serves as a condition, one instead sees the original moon.
All mundane phenomena are created by the mind; failing to recognize one's own mind, one claims that external objects exist.
The image within a mirror likewise has no real substance; with the mirror as a condition, one sees one's own face.
That which the mind grasps is also like this: not knowing it is one's own mind, one says that it exists apart from the mind.
If the image within a mirror were truly existent, why does it not go when seen departing,
or come when observed arriving?
Since that mirror is not real, all conventional phenomena are likewise so.
Sūtra: "One who knows thus... is called well-disciplined. Commentary:
This concludes the formal exposition.
*Vinaya* (the Discipline) refers to the ritual or norm that accords with the realization of *tathatā* (suchness) and the conventional world, for it is a wholesome standard to be followed.
"Discipline" (*vinaya*) means to subdue the three types of action (*trikarma*) and to bring all evils to rest.

To have a thorough knowledge of the nature of offenses, to be able to rely upon the roots of offenses, and to clearly recognize the characteristics of offenses so that they may be easily observed and uprooted is called "skillful discipline."
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the two bhikṣus arrived but were unable to speak.
The commentary states:
"The two manifest praise and glorification."
At first, he attained what he had never experienced before;
later, when his wisdom and eloquence were rightly praised, it was something Upāli could not equal.
The Sūtra says: "I then addressed him, [up to] 'arouse the thought of him as a householder.'"
The commentary states:
The Three Knowledges have already been announced; first was the general summary, and last will be the specific details.
This is the general announcement.
Sūtra: Why is this so? It is because his excellence is thus supreme. Commentary:
With the exception of the Buddha, no one is able to subdue the wisdom and eloquence of this Great Being; such are his wisdom and eloquence.
After some time, the two bhikṣus reached the state of a perfectly awakened mind (samyaksaṃbuddha-citta) and praised [the teaching], saying:
"The four [factors] manifest the extinction of offenses."
Although one has not yet realized the truth, by uprooting the seeds of transgression upon first hearing the wondrous principle, one should repent and bring them to cessation.
Not only are transgressions extinguished, but the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment is also awakened.
The Sūtra: He then paid homage and proceeded to the section on "Excellently Superior Wisdom and Eloquence.
Commentary:
Fifth, the description of making vows.
A newly ordained bhikṣu who has previously committed an offense, upon suddenly beholding such wisdom and eloquence—who would not pay him reverent homage?
Therefore, I prostrated before him.
After some time, I remained silent as I went to visit him regarding his illness.
The Epilogue states:
Having offered words of thanks, he humbly requests to withdraw.
This concludes the end of the third fascicle of the Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra.
